title: How to Comfort the Anxious and the Fearful
subtitle: On caring for the anxious in your church, ministering to fear and panic with both truth and patience, and the difference between rebuke and refuge

sections.title: The Affliction in Every Pew
sections.body:
It does not announce itself from the platform, but it is sitting in front of you in numbers that would frighten you if you knew them. The racing mind. The chest that tightens at three in the morning. The dread with no name. Anxiety is among the most common afflictions in your congregation, and most of the people carrying it have learned to hide it under a Sunday smile.

They are tired. Not lazy tired. The tired that comes from fighting your own mind all night.

We have not always served these people well. We have sometimes handed the anxious a verse about not worrying as though that settled it, and sent them home feeling both afraid and now guilty for being afraid. That is not comfort. That is a second weight laid on a person already buckling. The anxious do not need to be scolded for their fear. They need a shepherd patient enough to sit in the dark with them until the light comes up.

sections.title: Do Not Shame What God Does Not Shame
sections.body:
The first thing to kill is the instinct to treat anxiety as simple disobedience that a sufficiently spiritual person would not have. The Bible does not handle the fearful that way.

Elijah, having just called down fire from heaven, collapsed under a tree and asked to die. God did not lecture him. God fed him and let him sleep.

That is the pattern worth learning. The God of Scripture meets the afraid not with a rebuke but with provision, presence, and rest, and only then, gently, with the next step. The most frequent command in the Bible is do not be afraid, and it is never barked. It is always spoken into fear by a God drawing near, not standing back. So when an anxious believer comes to you, your face must not register impatience or surprise. It must register the patience of the One who fed Elijah, who calmed the storm, who told his frightened men to take heart. Shame the fear and you drive the person back into hiding. Sit with the fear, and you may earn the right to speak peace into it.

sections.title: Anxiety Is Not Only a Spiritual Problem
sections.body:
We do the anxious a disservice when we treat their struggle as purely a matter of weak faith, because we are not only souls. We are also bodies, and the two are woven together more tightly than our theology usually admits.

Elijah's first cure was not a sermon. It was food and sleep.

The man who has not slept, who is drowning in caffeine and screens, who carries trauma in his nervous system, who has a genuine medical condition, will not be helped by being told to pray harder. Sometimes the most pastoral counsel is to eat, rest, walk, breathe, and yes, when needed, to see a doctor, and to tell the anxious that doing so is not a failure of faith. The God who made the body is not insulted when we tend it. So minister to the whole person. Pray with them, surely, and also ask when they last slept and whether they have eaten and whether they have anyone to talk to. Comfort that ignores the body is not more spiritual. It is just incomplete, and the anxious can tell the difference.

sections.title: What the Fearful Actually Need to Hear
sections.body:
After patience, after care for the body, the anxious still need the deep thing, the truth that holds when the feelings will not. And the truth is not be calm. The truth is that they are held.

Fear says you are alone and it is all on you. The gospel says neither is true.

The anxious mind preaches a relentless sermon of isolation and catastrophe, and it cannot be argued out of the sufferer by force. But it can be slowly answered, over time, by a better word. Cast your anxiety on him, Peter writes, because he cares for you. The reason given is not because anxiety is wrong. It is because he cares. That is the anchor. Not a command to stop feeling, but a Person to feel it toward, a God who invites the whole crushing weight to be handed over because he is strong enough to carry it and loving enough to want to. So speak that, patiently and repeatedly, into the fearful heart. Remind them where the burden can go. The peace that guards them, Paul says, surpasses understanding, which means it does not wait for the circumstances to make sense. It is given in the dark, to the afraid, by a God who never once told a frightened person to figure it out alone.

sections.title: Comfort Others With the Comfort You Received
sections.body:
I cannot write this from above it. I have lain awake with my own dread, certain of disasters that never came, ashamed that a man who preaches faith should be so well acquainted with fear.

The shepherds who comfort the anxious best are the ones who have walked through the valley themselves and remember the cold of it.

Paul said God comforts us in our troubles so that we can comfort others with the comfort we ourselves received. The supply of comfort you have to give your people runs exactly as deep as the comfort you have received in your own affliction, and not an inch deeper. So do not hide your own fears from God in order to keep up appearances before your flock. Take them to him. Let him meet you under your own tree, with food and rest and a quieter word, and then carry what he gives you to the trembling people in your pews. They do not need a pastor who has never been afraid. They need one who was, and who found that the everlasting arms were underneath the whole time, and who can say with the weight of experience that they will hold. Go and sit with the anxious. You know the way. You have been down that road, and you came back.
